title: Spatial Disorientation, Illusions, and the Vestibular System

questions.text: In IMC, the aircraft enters a gradual left bank at 1°/second undetected by the pilot. After 30 seconds (30° of unperceived bank), the pilot notices the attitude indicator showing a 30° left bank and corrects rapidly back to wings-level. What sensation does the pilot now experience and what is the critical error to avoid?

options.label: A
options.text: The pilot experiences 'the leans' — a strong sensation of banking to the RIGHT, even though the aircraft is actually wings-level; the rapid correction to wings-level was detected by the semicircular canals as a rightward rotation, convincing the brain the aircraft is now banked right; the critical error to avoid: adjusting the aircraft toward the false sensation (rolling left to feel 'level') would reintroduce the actual left bank; the pilot must trust the attitude indicator and hold wings-level despite the compelling sensation of right bank

options.label: B
options.text: The pilot feels a leftward banking sensation — the rapid correction to the right was detected by the left semicircular canal, creating a sensation of continued left bank; the pilot must now add more right aileron to overcome the lingering sensation; the attitude indicator will lag the correction and eventually align with the true wings-level attitude

options.label: C
options.text: The pilot feels completely level — once the attitude indicator shows wings-level and the aircraft is confirmed wings-level, the vestibular system rapidly recalibrates to the new attitude; the leans are only experienced when the correction is made in the same direction as the original bank, not when the correction is opposite

options.label: D
options.text: The pilot experiences vertigo — a spinning sensation caused by the rapid correction that stimulates all three semicircular canals simultaneously; the correct response is to close the eyes and rely on total body awareness to maintain attitude until the spinning sensation stops

questions.explanation: This question traces the exact neurological sequence of the leans. Step 1: The 30° gradual left bank at 1°/sec occurred below the semicircular canal detection threshold (approximately 2°/sec for sustained rotation). No signal sent to the brain — the pilot PERCEIVES wings-level despite being banked 30° left. Step 2: The rapid correction to wings-level causes a rightward rotation at above-threshold speed. The right semicircular canal detects this motion. Step 3: The brain receives a rightward rotation signal. Combined with the prior 'wings-level' reference state, the brain concludes the aircraft is now banked RIGHT. Step 4: The attitude indicator shows wings-level. The body says banked right. This conflict — instrument vs. body — IS the leans. The leans sensation is neurologically compelling and very difficult to override by willpower alone. It typically persists for 1-3 minutes as the endolymph in the semicircular canals slowly returns to rest. The CRITICAL ERROR: adjusting the aircraft toward the false sensation. If the pilot rolls left to relieve the right-bank feeling, the actual aircraft reintroduces a left bank — the scenario from Step 1 begins again, now compounding with accumulated bank. Trust the AI. Hold the correction. Wait for the sensation to subside. The 'vertigo' answer's 'close eyes' advice is the worst possible guidance — closing eyes removes all instrument reference and maximizes the risk of control loss.

questions.text: A VFR pilot inadvertently flies into IMC in mountainous terrain. After approximately 90 seconds, the pilot notices a descending airspeed increase from 100 to 125 knots. The pilot is disoriented and pulls back on the yoke aggressively. The airspeed continues to increase to 145 knots and the altitude continues dropping. What is occurring?

options.label: A
options.text: Structural failure is imminent — at 145 knots in turbulent mountain IMC, the aircraft is approaching Va (maneuvering speed); the pilot should immediately reduce power to idle and release back pressure to prevent overstress; allowing the aircraft to seek its own level flight attitude from neutral controls will recover the spiral automatically

options.label: B
options.text: The aircraft has entered a power-on stall — the airspeed increase to 145 knots is a false reading from a blocked pitot tube; the real airspeed is decreasing toward stall; pulling back is correct as it reduces the angle of attack; the pilot should continue pulling back and add full power to arrest the stall

options.label: C
options.text: The aircraft has entered a graveyard spiral — the pilot is likely in an undetected banked attitude; pulling back on the elevator in a banked aircraft does not level the flight path — it tightens the turn and increases G-loading; the centripetal acceleration of the turn combined with elevator back pressure creates a progressively steepener spiral; airspeed and altitude loss continue to increase; correct recovery: level the wings FIRST using partial panel instruments (TC + altimeter), THEN apply back pressure to break the descent

options.label: D
options.text: The aircraft is experiencing a phugoid oscillation — pulling back momentarily increases pitch and slows the aircraft before the oscillation reverses; continuing back pressure for 10-15 seconds will arrest the phugoid cycle; the pilot should hold back pressure and wait for the pitch oscillation to dampen naturally

questions.explanation: The graveyard spiral is the exact scenario being described: (1) VFR pilot in IMC → 90 seconds → spatial disorientation. (2) Undetected bank → nose drops → airspeed increases (the slipstream indicator of an unnoticed descent rather than a climb). (3) Pilot notices descent, pulls back. (4) Pulling back in a BANKED aircraft applies back pressure to the elevator → creates centripetal acceleration → tightens the turn → the aircraft turns faster and descends faster. (5) Results: airspeed CONTINUES to increase, altitude CONTINUES to fall — the back pressure made it WORSE, not better. Why pulling back accelerates the spiral in a bank: in a 45° bank, approximately 1.41 G is needed just for level flight (the load factor curve). Back pressure beyond this adds centripetal acceleration to an already banked track. The control input needed by the pilot to escape: (1) Focus on the turn coordinator. Level the bank indicator first. (2) Once wings-level confirmed: gradually apply back pressure to stop the descent. (3) All in partial panel (AI and HI may be unavailable if vacuum has failed). The NTSB statistic: the average unrated VFR pilot loses control in IMC in 178 seconds. This scenario occurs at 90 seconds — well within statistical precedent. The 'structural failure is imminent' answer (release back pressure) is partially correct — releasing back pressure in a bank stops the descent-acceleration from back pressure, but the bank must be corrected first.

questions.text: A pilot approaches an unfamiliar airport at night from over dark, featureless water (a black hole approach). The airport has a VASI system showing 3 red and 1 white (3R/1W). What does this VASI indication mean and what should the pilot do?

options.label: A
options.text: 3 red and 1 white on a PAPI means the aircraft is above the glidepath — red lights indicate higher than glidepath; white lights indicate lower; 3 red and 1 white means the aircraft is slightly high; reduce power to descend to 2R/2W

options.label: B
options.text: 3 red and 1 white on a VASI is a system malfunction — a properly functioning VASI can only show 2 red or 2 white lights, never a 3:1 combination; declare radio failure and request ATC radar vectors for the approach

options.label: C
options.text: 3 red / 1 white means the aircraft is below the glidepath — 4 red means dangerously low, 4 white means too high; the pilot should add power and climb to achieve the correct 2R/2W on-glidepath indication

options.label: D
options.text: A 2-bar VASI uses color combinations per bar, not per light; 3 red and 1 white is not a standard VASI reading — the standard 2-bar VASI shows either both bars red (too low), near bar red/far bar white (on glidepath), or both bars white (too high); the pilot may be observing a PAPI system, which uses 4 individual lights; for a PAPI: 3 red and 1 white means the aircraft is BELOW glidepath and must climb; the only correct on-glidepath PAPI indication is 2R/2W

questions.explanation: This question requires distinguishing between the VASI (Visual Approach Slope Indicator) and PAPI (Precision Approach Path Indicator) systems. Standard 2-bar VASI: uses TWO light bars — a near bar and a far bar. Each bar shows red (below glidepath for that bar's reference angle) or white (above glidepath reference). Readings: Both bars RED → below glidepath (too low). Near bar RED / Far bar WHITE → on glidepath (correct). Both bars WHITE → above glidepath (too high). A 2-bar VASI cannot produce '3 red 1 white' because it has only 2 bars — one per side. PAPI System: uses 4 INDIVIDUAL light units in a row. Each unit shows red (below glidepath) or white (above glidepath) based on that unit's angle. PAPI readings: 4 white → well above glidepath. 3 white 1 red → slightly above. 2 white 2 red → ON glidepath. 1 white 3 red → slightly below. 4 red → well below. CONCLUSION: '3 red 1 white' is a PAPI indication of BELOW glidepath, not a VASI indication. The pilot must raise the nose/add power to achieve 2R/2W. Critical for the night black hole: the visual impression is that the aircraft is approaching too HIGH (featureless dark terrain makes the runway look lower) — the PAPI shows the actual geometric truth, which is too LOW. Trust the PAPI. The 'PAPI shows above glidepath' answer inverts the meaning of PAPI colors: red = BELOW glidepath (too low), white = ABOVE glidepath (too high).

questions.text: During a night visual approach, a pilot executes a go-around at 50 feet AGL. Full power is applied. The pilot immediately feels the aircraft's nose pitching up steeply — almost vertically. The pilot pushes forward on the yoke to correct the perceived excessive nose-high attitude. What is the most dangerous outcome of this action?

options.label: A
options.text: Pushing forward raises the tail and reduces lift from the wing root, which increases stall speed; at 50 feet AGL the aircraft is too slow for nose-down pitch input; the pilot should maintain back pressure and allow the aircraft to climb through the illusion at the cost of a slightly longer ground roll

options.label: B
options.text: The nose-high feeling during a go-around is the leans — caused by the rapid change in heading from the traffic pattern to the go-around runway alignment; the correct response is the same as for the leans: trust the instruments; pushing forward is acceptable if the attitude indicator confirms nose-high attitude

options.label: C
options.text: Pushing forward during the go-around corrects the excessive nose-high attitude — the pilot is right to push forward; at 50 feet AGL on a go-around, an excessive nose-high attitude would cause an early stall; forward pressure prevents the stall and is the correct instinctive response

options.label: D
options.text: The perceived nose-high attitude at full power application is the somatogravic illusion — the otolith organs interpret forward linear G-force from rapid acceleration as a pitch-up; the aircraft may be at a NORMAL or slightly nose-high go-around attitude; pushing forward reduces pitch below level flight at 50 feet AGL and causes the aircraft to descend into the runway or terrain during the go-around; this is a controlled flight into terrain (CFIT) scenario that has produced fatal accidents

questions.explanation: The somatogravic illusion during a night go-around is a documented CFIT accident mechanism. The neurological sequence: (1) Go-around initiated from 50 feet AGL — full power applied. (2) Aircraft accelerates rapidly from slow final approach speed to go-around power. (3) The linear forward acceleration (G-force forward) stimulates the otolith organs (utricle) — the same organs that detect upward linear G in a pitch-up. (4) The brain interprets the forward G as a pitch-up (nose-high) rotation. (5) The pilot perceives an almost vertical nose-up attitude when the actual pitch may be 10-15° nose-high (normal go-around). (6) Instinctive correction: push forward. (7) At 50 feet AGL with go-around speed (around 65-75 knots depending on the aircraft), a nose-down input that reduces angle of attack below wings-level can cause descent into the runway or terrain in less than 2 seconds. CFIT from this illusion has occurred at airports and on missed approaches in IMC with identical mechanisms. Prevention: at night/IMC go-around, the pilot must be pre-briefed: 'EXPECT A PITCH-UP SENSATION AT FULL POWER — RESIST FORWARD INPUT — TRUST ATTITUDE INDICATOR.' This requires deliberate pre-go-around preparation, not in-the-moment recognition. The 'this is the leans' answer misidentifies the illusion as 'the leans' — the mechanism is entirely different (otolith linear acceleration vs. semicircular canal rotation detection).

questions.text: Approaching an unfamiliar airport for the first time at night, the pilot notices the runway appears narrow relative to their home runway. Given this visual cue, how will the pilot likely perceive the approach and how should they compensate?

options.label: A
options.text: The narrow runway provides no depth cue information — visual width is irrelevant to approach angle perception; the pilot makes the same approach to a narrow and wide runway using the same visual cues (horizon relationship, runway proportions); no compensation is required

options.label: B
options.text: The narrow runway will appear FARTHER AWAY and LOWER than the home airport runway — the narrow width contains fewer width-based depth cues, making it appear more distant and at a lower position relative to the pilot's eye; the pilot will tend to fly an approach that appears correct but is actually TOO LOW; compensation: use VASI/PAPI as the primary glidepath reference; disregard the visual impression of approach angle and trust the electronic glidepath indicator

options.label: C
options.text: The narrow runway will appear CLOSER than the home airport — the denser visual pattern of a narrower runway creates more depth cue compression than a wide runway, causing the pilot to perceive shorter distance; the pilot will tend to fly HIGH and should reduce power to compensate

options.label: D
options.text: The narrow runway requires the pilot to fly HIGHER — because the runway appears lower than actual, the pilot must consciously aim above what feels correct; if the VASI shows on-glidepath and the runway appears slightly low, the VASI is compensating for the narrow runway illusion and should be disregarded in favor of the visual impression

questions.explanation: The narrow runway illusion is one of the most operationally significant visual approach illusions because it produces an UNDERSTATED glidepath — the pilot is lower than they perceive. The mechanism: human depth and size perception uses width as a primary visual cue for distance estimation. The pilot's visual system has calibrated 'normal runway width' from their home airport or most frequently flown airports. When approaching a narrower runway, the width subtends a smaller visual angle than expected at the same distance → the brain's depth estimation system interprets this smaller-than-expected width as 'the runway is farther away than it looks' → further objects appear lower → the pilot believes they are HIGH when they are actually ON or BELOW glidepath → the pilot descends to 'correct' the perceived high approach → the aircraft is now BELOW glidepath. Runway width-related CFIT is documented in FAA accident records. The correct compensation is to use VASI/PAPI, ILS glideslope, or GPS vertical guidance as the primary reference and explicitly discount the visual glidepath impression at unfamiliar airports. The 'fly higher' answer inverts the compensation direction — 'fly higher because the runway appears lower' would actually be correct if the pilot did not have VASI/PAPI reference, but D then tells the pilot to disregard the VASI, which is dangerously wrong.

questions.text: A VFR pilot is 45 minutes from destination when the weather deteriorates ahead. Visibility ahead is reported as 1.5 miles in mist. The ceiling is forecast at 800 feet AGL and descending. The pilot thinks: 'I've been in worse than this. I'll stay low and slow under the clouds. My destination has a hotel — I'll make it.' Identify the hazardous attitude(s) and the correct ADM response.

options.label: A
options.text: Multiple hazardous attitudes are present — Get-There-Itis (destination fixation overriding weather decision), Invulnerability (I've done this before), and potentially Macho (scoffing at 'worse conditions'); the correct ADM response: (1) land at the nearest airport NOW before entering deteriorating conditions; (2) check weather for alternate routing or improving conditions; (3) if the ceiling drops to 800 feet during a 45-minute flight at 100+ knots, the pilot may find themselves in IMC with no instrument rating and no escape; (4) a VFR pilot who enters IMC statistically has less than 3 minutes before losing control; the hotel at the destination has no value if the pilot does not survive the flight

options.label: B
options.text: The pilot should divert to the alternate airport listed on the VFR flight plan — all VFR flight plans require an alternate airport listing; the alternate airport is the legal and appropriate response when the destination weather is below VFR minimums; continue toward the alternate at cruise altitude

options.label: C
options.text: The pilot is correct — maintaining VFR below clouds at 800 feet at reduced speed is a legal and safe operation; 14 CFR 91.155 requires 1 mile visibility and 500 feet below clouds in Class G; if the weather stays above 800 feet ceiling and 1.5 miles, the flight is legal; the pilot should continue and monitor

options.label: D
options.text: The pilot should climb above the clouds — at reported ceiling of 800 feet, climbing to an altitude above the cloud tops would provide VMC on top; once above the clouds, proceed to destination and then check weather for descent; this is a Class G airspace operation that does not require IFR rating

questions.explanation: This scenario presents a classic VFR-into-IMC setup with multiple hazardous attitudes driving the pilot toward a fatal decision. Hazardous attitude identification: (1) GET-THERE-ITIS: the hotel at the destination is explicitly mentioned as a motivating factor — this is the textbook pressure that overrides weather conservatism decisions. FAA studies identify destination fixation as the primary cause of VFR-into-IMC accidents. (2) INVULNERABILITY: 'I've been in worse than this' — past success in marginal conditions falsely validates the risk of repeating the behavior. (3) MACHO: implied confidence ('I'll make it') that discounts the actual physical hazard. The correct ADM: the weather is CURRENTLY 1.5 miles and 800 feet AGL ceiling and FORECAST TO DESCEND. The pilot is 45 minutes from the destination. At 100 knots, that is 75 miles. Forecasted ceiling descent means conditions at the destination may be below VFR legal minimums by arrival — even if marginal legal now. The pilot should: LAND NOW at the nearest suitable airport before the weather deteriorates further. Call ahead to destination, check METARs and TAFs, and wait for improving conditions or arrange ground transportation. The 'maintaining VFR below the clouds is fine' answer invokes the legal dimensional minimums but ignores the FORECAST trend — deteriorating conditions are not 'safe' conditions even when momentarily above minimums. The 'climb above the clouds' answer (climb on top) is extremely dangerous (how does the VFR pilot descend through IMC on top?). The spatial disorientation connection: a VFR pilot in IMC with 1.5 miles visibility and 800 ft ceiling can enter complete IMC from a single degree of inadvertent heading change into a cloud wall.
questions.sjt_rationale: Get-There-Itis is statistically the primary kill mechanism in VFR-into-IMC accidents. The emotional stakes (destination, hotel, plans) override objective weather assessment. The correct antidote per FAA: HAVE A PLAN TO STOP. Pre-commit to a weather personal minimum (e.g., '3 miles and 1,500 AGL minimum') and honor it regardless of perceived pressure.

questions.text: What is the correct control sequence for recovering from a graveyard spiral when only partial panel instruments are available (attitude indicator and heading indicator are unreliable after vacuum failure)?

options.label: A
options.text: Call ATC immediately and request a radar heading to level — without reliable attitude instruments, attempting to self-recover from a spiral will worsen the spatial disorientation; ATC radar vectors provide external heading confirmation; fly the ATC-assigned heading until the vacuum system self-restores

options.label: B
options.text: Level the wings FIRST using the turn coordinator (verify bank direction from TC), then gradually apply back pressure to break the descent — in a graveyard spiral, the back pressure alone (without first leveling wings) increases the G-loading in the bank and tightens the spiral; the sequence is non-negotiable: LEVEL FIRST, THEN PULL

options.label: C
options.text: Reduce power to idle first — the spiral is driven by excess power; reducing to idle will reduce airspeed and naturally reduce the bank/descent coupling; once the airspeed drops below Va, apply back pressure and level simultaneously

options.label: D
options.text: Apply full back pressure immediately and simultaneously level the wings — the spiral requires both corrections at once; sequential actions take too long at altitude near terrain; apply both simultaneously using maximum control input to stop the descent as quickly as possible

questions.explanation: The graveyard spiral recovery sequence is specific, sequential, and non-negotiable: (1) LEVEL THE WINGS FIRST. Use the turn coordinator (TC is electrically powered and survives vacuum failure). The TC shows: level wings (no deflection of the wings of the miniature aircraft), rate of turn (standard rate = ball at the index), and the inclinometer (ball). Level the wings until the TC miniature aircraft wings are level and the ball is centered. (2) THEN APPLY BACK PRESSURE to stop the descent. Once the aircraft is wings-level, back pressure applies correctly as nose-up pitch — not as tightening centripetal acceleration in a turn. At this point the altitude is recovered with a normal pull-up. PARTIAL PANEL: the AI and HI are unreliable (vacuum failure) — do NOT use them. The TC is the sole attitude reference for bank. The altimeter confirms descent rate after wings-level. Why sequence matters: back pressure before wings-level in a bank = higher G → higher stall speed → possible accelerated stall at low altitude → an accelerated stall from a graveyard spiral at terrain level is non-survivable. Level the wings to eliminate the centripetal loading FIRST, then convert the remaining airspeed into altitude with back pressure. The 'simultaneous back-pressure and wing-level' answer (simultaneous back + wing level) is the SECOND BEST approach — getting wings-level is still higher priority than back pressure, but simultaneous application is less dangerous than back pressure first. The strict sequence is the taught recovery method.

questions.text: During a night cross-country, a pilot executes a missed approach from 200 feet AGL over dark terrain (no visible lights nearby). At full power on the go-around, the pilot feels a strong nose-high sensation and consciously thinks: 'This must be the somatogravic illusion — I should trust the AI.' The attitude indicator shows 15° nose-up and 90 knots. The pilot holds the attitude and climbs. Was this the correct response?

options.label: A
options.text: No — the pilot should have pushed forward regardless of the AI reading; if the somatogravic illusion is suspected, the correct response is always to push forward to a neutral pitch attitude; trusting the AI at night may compound the illusion through instrument fixation

options.label: B
options.text: Partially — the pilot should have trusted the AI for pitch but used the altimeter to confirm rate of climb before committing to the go-around climb; 15° nose-up without altimeter confirmation may still be too high and the pilot should adjust to 10° nose-up and monitor the VSI

options.label: C
options.text: Yes — recognizing the somatogravic illusion and explicitly deciding to trust the attitude indicator is precisely the correct response; at 15° nose-up and 90 knots, the aircraft is in a normal go-around climb attitude; the AI confirms a safe pitch attitude; holding the nose-up attitude on AI authority while resisting the push-forward instinct is the correct and complete ADM chain that prevents the CFIT scenario caused by acting on the illusion

options.label: D
options.text: No — a 15° nose-up attitude at 90 knots is excessive and approaching a stall; the pilot correctly felt a too-steep climb; the somatogravic illusion should be suspected only when the AI shows less than 10° nose-up; above 10°, trust the body sensation, not the illusion diagnosis

questions.explanation: This scenario specifically tests whether the student has internalized the complete ADM chain for the somatogravic illusion — not just knowing the term, but executing the correct response when the body sensation is active and compelling. The pilot's response sequence: (1) Felt nose-high sensation — experienced the illusion. (2) Named it — 'this must be the somatogravic illusion.' (3) Explicitly decided to trust the AI — application of Aeronautical Decision Making. (4) AI confirms 15° nose-up, 90 knots — a normal go-around attitude for most light aircraft (Vy speed, positive pitch, climbing). (5) Held the attitude — resisted the push-forward instinct. This is the CORRECT and COMPLETE response. The danger is in steps 2 and 3: most pilots in actual night go-arounds do not reach step 2 (naming the illusion) because the sensation is immediate and overwhelming. This is why the somatogravic illusion training requires PROACTIVE PREPARATION before the go-around — the pilot must have pre-briefed: 'If I apply full power at night, I will feel excessive nose-up. I will trust the AI.' The 'push forward regardless of the AI' answer inverts the solution — pushing forward regardless of AI reading would cause CFIT. The 'above 10 degrees, trust your body' answer invents an 'above 10° trust your body' threshold that has no physiological or regulatory basis. 15° nose-up at 90 knots in a go-around is a standard, safe attitude — the body sensation is wrong, the AI is right.
questions.sjt_rationale: This is a positive ADM scenario — the pilot DID the right thing. Testing comprehension of why it was right, and making sure students understand the complete chain: Recognition → Naming → Explicit instrument trust → Hold the attitude. The student who cannot explain WHY it was correct cannot reliably reproduce it under real-time night-flight pressure.
